TMJ, Muscles of Mastication & Trigeminal Nerve

The temporomandibular joint and its movements, the four muscles of mastication, and the three divisions of CN V with their dental blocks.

Lecture 8 · Part 1The Mandible

Lecturer: Dr Nur Hassan, BDS, PGT (Oral Surg), PhD — Senior Lecturer, CSU.

  • The strongest, largest bone of the face
  • Left and right parts fused in the middle
  • Has a buccal and lingual plate and an alveolar arch
RegionFeatures
SymphysisSuperior and inferior mental (genial) spines
ParasymphysisThe region either side of the midline
BodyMental foramen, mylohyoid line, sublingual and submandibular fossae, retromolar trigone
AngleThe junction of body and ramus
RamusCondylar process (head and neck) and coronoid process

Lecture 8 · Part 2Muscles of Mastication

  • All originate on the skull and insert on the mandible
  • All are derivatives of the 1st branchial arch
  • All are innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3)
  • They move the mandible: elevation, depression, protrusion, retrusion and lateral excursion
The four muscles
MasseterTemporalisMedial pterygoidLateral pterygoid
Careful: buccinator is not a muscle of mastication — it is a muscle of facial expression supplied by CN VII, even though it helps keep the bolus on the occlusal table.

Masseter

  • A powerful muscle of mastication, and one of the main postural muscles at rest
  • Origin — superficial head (larger): inferior border of the anterior ⅔ of the zygomatic arch
  • Origin — deep head: medial border of the zygomatic arch and the inferior border of the posterior ⅓
  • Insertion: lateral surface of the ramus and the angle of the mandible
  • Action: elevation (major action); assists protrusion, retrusion and lateral gliding
  • Nerve: masseteric branch of V3

Temporalis

  • Large, fan shaped — the most powerful muscle of mastication, and a main postural muscle
  • Origin: temporal fossa, along the inferior temporal line
  • Insertion: coronoid process and anterior border of the ramus
  • Action: elevation (anterior fibres) and retrusion (posterior fibres); also protraction and side-to-side motion
  • Nerve: anterior and posterior deep temporal branches of V3
  • Fascia: temporoparietal fascia, plus superficial and deep layers of temporalis fascia
Fibre direction explains function: the anterior fibres run vertically, so they elevate; the posterior fibres run almost horizontally, so they pull the mandible backwards.

Medial pterygoid

  • Origin — superficial head: maxillary tuberosity and the pyramidal process of the palatine bone
  • Origin — deep head: medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and the pterygoid fossa
  • Insertion: medial surface of the mandibular ramus
  • Action: elevation (major action); assists lateral gliding
  • Nerve: nerve to medial pterygoid, a branch of V3
The sling: masseter on the outside and medial pterygoid on the inside form a muscular sling around the angle of the mandible — which is why they act together so powerfully in elevation.

Lateral pterygoid

HeadOriginInsertion
Upper headRoof of the infratemporal fossa — the infratemporal crest of the greater wing of the sphenoidArticular disc and capsule of the TMJ
Lower head (larger)Lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid platePterygoid fovea on the neck of the mandibular condyle
  • Action: depresses and protrudes the mandible; lateral excursion
  • Nerve: nerve to lateral pterygoid, a branch of V3
The odd one out: lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that opens the jaw. Its attachment to the articular disc is also why it matters so much in TMJ dysfunction — it pulls the disc forward as the condyle translates.

Blood supply & venous drainage

  • Arterial: branches of the maxillary artery and the superficial temporal artery, both from the external carotid
  • Venous: the pterygoid plexus, middle temporal and transverse facial veins
  • The anterior and posterior deep temporal, masseteric, pterygoid and buccal veins all join the pterygoid plexus

Lecture 8 · Part 3The Temporomandibular Joint

Definition: the articulation between the squamous portion of the temporal bone and the condyle of the mandible.

Components
Articular eminenceMandibular (glenoid) fossaHead of the mandibular condyle Articular discCapsuleExtracapsular ligaments
Movement typeProduces
HingeElevation and depression
Gliding (translation)Protrusion and retraction
Pivoting (rotation)Unilateral side-to-side movement

Function: opening and closing the mouth, chewing, and side-to-side movement of the lower jaw.

Mandibular fossa

  • The mandibular (glenoid) fossa is a hollow on the inferior surface of the squamous temporal bone
  • Bounded anteriorly by a ridge of bone, the articular eminence, which forms the anterior margin of the joint
  • The petrotympanic fissure lies behind — the chorda tympani (a branch of CN VII) passes through it

Joint compartments

Upper compartment

  • Gliding movement — protrusion and retraction

Lower compartment

  • Hinge movement — depression and elevation
  • Articular surfaces are lined by fibrocartilage — not hyaline cartilage
  • Non-articular surfaces are lined by synovial membrane
Two features make the TMJ unusual: its articular surfaces are covered in fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage, and it is one of the few joints with an articular disc dividing it into two functionally separate compartments.

Articular disc

  • A biconcave sheet of avascular fibrous connective tissue
  • Anteriorly it blends with fibres of the lateral pterygoid
  • Posteriorly it attaches to loose connective tissue — the bilaminar zone, which contains nerves
  • Lined by synovial membrane, producing synovial fluid
  • Separates the joint into superior (translation) and inferior (rotation) compartments
  • Functions: movement, cushioning, stability and proprioception
Why TMJ pain localises where it does: the disc itself is avascular and largely aneural, but the bilaminar zone behind it is richly innervated — so posterior displacement of the condyle onto that tissue is painful.

Ligaments

LigamentAttachmentsRole
Lateral ligamentRoot of the zygoma → posterior aspect of the condylar neckLimits joint movement
SphenomandibularSpine of the sphenoid → internal part of the ramus, near the lingulaLimits maximum opening of the jaw
StylomandibularStyloid process → angle and internal part of the mandibleLimits extreme protrusion
Collateral ligamentsConnect the medial and lateral aspects of the articular discAnchor the disc to the condyle

Neurovascular supply of the joint

Arteries

  • Superficial temporal artery — branch of the ECA
  • Deep auricular and anterior tympanic arteries — branches of the maxillary artery

Veins

  • Superficial temporal and maxillary veins, draining into the retromandibular vein

Nerves — all from V3

  • Auriculotemporal nerve
  • Masseteric nerve
  • Posterior deep temporal nerve
Referred pain: because the auriculotemporal nerve supplies both the TMJ and the skin of the external ear and auditory meatus, TMJ problems are frequently reported by patients as earache.

Lecture 8 · Part 4Trigeminal Nerve — Overview

DivisionModalityExit from the skull
Ophthalmic (V1)Sensory onlySuperior orbital fissure
Maxillary (V2)Sensory onlyForamen rotundum
Mandibular (V3)Motor and sensoryForamen ovale

The trigeminal ganglion sits in Meckel’s cave in the middle cranial fossa.

Mnemonic: Standing Room Only — Superior orbital fissure (V1), foramen Rotundum (V2), foramen Ovale (V3).

Ophthalmic nerve (V1)

  • Runs within the middle cranial fossa, in the cavernous sinus
  • Gives a meningeal branch to the dura of the middle cranial fossa
  • Three major branches pass through the superior orbital fissure to enter the orbit
BranchSub-branchesSupplies
Lacrimal—Upper eyelid (skin, conjunctiva) and the lacrimal gland (sensory and parasympathetic)
FrontalSupraorbital, supratrochlearUpper eyelid (skin, conjunctiva) and the skin of the forehead
NasociliaryShort ciliarySensory fibres of the ciliary ganglion
Long ciliaryCornea and sclera
Posterior ethmoidalEthmoid air cells and sphenoid sinus
Anterior ethmoidalInternal nasal branch → anterior nasal cavity; external nasal branch → skin of the nose
InfratrochlearMedial aspect of the upper eyelid (skin, conjunctiva) and the lacrimal sac

Maxillary nerve (V2)

  • Passes through the cavernous sinus, giving a middle meningeal branch to the meninges
  • Enters foramen rotundum and reaches the pterygopalatine fossa
  • Continues anteriorly through the infraorbital fissure and the infraorbital canal as the infraorbital nerve, exiting via the infraorbital foramen
BranchSupplies
In the pterygopalatine fossa
Zygomatic → zygomaticotemporalSkin of the temple region
Zygomatic → zygomaticofacialSkin of the cheek
Posterior superior alveolarMaxillary 8, 7 and 6 (distobuccal and palatal roots)
Ganglionic branchesPass through the pterygopalatine ganglion
In the infraorbital canal
Middle superior alveolarMaxillary 6 (mesiobuccal root), 5 and 4
Anterior superior alveolarMaxillary 1, 2 and 3
On the face
InfraorbitalLower eyelid and infraorbital skin

Branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion

BranchRouteSupplies
Orbital branchVia the superior orbital fissureOrbital periosteum, ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses
Nasopalatine nerveSphenopalatine foramen → nasopalatine canalAnterior hard palate and inferior nasal septum
Posterior superior nasalSphenopalatine foramenNasal cavity
Greater and lesser palatinePalatine canalHard and soft palate
Pharyngeal nervePalatovaginal canalNasopharynx

Lecture 8 · Part 5Mandibular Nerve (V3)

V3 sensory

  • Teeth and gingiva
  • Anterior ⅔ of the tongue
  • Mucosa of the floor of the oral cavity
  • Lower lip
  • Skin of the temple and lower face
  • Part of the cranial dura mater

V3 motor

  • Muscles of mastication
  • Tensor tympani — in the middle ear
  • Tensor veli palatini — of the soft palate
  • (also mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric)
V3 is the only division with a motor root. V1 and V2 are purely sensory.

Course

  • Originates from the trigeminal ganglion in the middle cranial fossa
  • Passes through foramen ovale to reach the infratemporal fossa
  • Passes between tensor veli palatini and the upper head of lateral pterygoid
  • The small motor root passes medial to the trigeminal ganglion, through foramen ovale, and immediately joins the sensory part

Branches

TrunkBranchSupplies
From the main trunk
MainMeningeal branchAscends and enters foramen spinosum; sensory to the dura of the middle cranial fossa and the mastoid air cells
MainNerve to medial pterygoidMedial pterygoid, tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani
Anterior trunk — mainly motor
AnteriorLong buccal nerveBuccal gingivae of the lower molars, skin of the cheek and buccal mucous membrane (sensory)
AnteriorMasseteric nerveMasseter and the TMJ
AnteriorDeep temporal nerves (×2)Temporalis
AnteriorNerve to lateral pterygoidLateral pterygoid
Posterior trunk — mainly sensory
PosteriorAuriculotemporal nerveSkin over the temple; external ear, external auditory meatus, tympanic membrane and the TMJ; carries parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland after relay in the otic ganglion
PosteriorLingual nerveAnterior ⅔ of the tongue, floor of the mouth, lingual gingivae of the lower teeth
PosteriorInferior alveolar nerveMandibular teeth — see below

Lingual nerve & its hitchhikers

  • Lingual nerve (sensory, V3): anterior ⅔ of the tongue, oral mucosa of the floor of the mouth, lingual gingivae of the lower teeth
  • Chorda tympani — a branch of the facial nerve that joins the lingual nerve, carrying taste from the anterior ⅔ of the tongue and parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands
Two errors on this slide. It lists the lesser petrosal nerve as “a branch of the facial nerve” that “joins with the lingual nerve”. In fact the lesser petrosal nerve is a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) — as the slide’s own heading says — and it does not join the lingual nerve. It runs to the otic ganglion, and the postganglionic fibres reach the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. The parotid parasympathetic pathway is IX → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal.

Inferior alveolar nerve

  • Enters the mandibular foramen and travels along the mandibular canal
  • Supplies the molars and second premolars
BranchDetail
Nerve to mylohyoidGiven off just before the nerve enters the mandibular foramen; descends in a groove on the lingual side of the ramus; supplies mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric, and gives accessory sensory innervation to the mandibular teeth
Incisive nerveContinues in the mandibular canal to supply the first premolar, canine and incisors
Mental nerveExits through the mental foramen; supplies the lower lip, chin and labial gingiva
Why the mylohyoid nerve matters clinically: because it branches off before the mandibular foramen, it escapes an inferior alveolar nerve block — and its accessory supply to the mandibular teeth is one reason an IANB sometimes fails to give full pulpal anaesthesia.
IAN injury: the roots of a lower third molar may lie against or wrap around the mandibular canal, so removing it carries a risk of temporary or permanent altered sensation of the lower lip and chin. This is a standard consent point before surgical extraction.
Typo in the summary table: it says the lingual nerve carries “taste sensations to the anterior third of tongue”. It is the anterior two-thirds — and the taste fibres belong to the chorda tympani (CN VII), which merely travels with the lingual nerve.
